Illustrative example only. It isn't financial advice and uses no current tax rates or official values.

How this works

Profit is what you earn minus what you spend. Cash is what is in the bank. The two drift apart when your customers pay you later than you pay your suppliers.

The explorer uses the same sales and costs every month for 6 months, starting in month 1, and counts each month as 30 days. A payment arrives a whole number of months later: 0 days is the same month, 1 to 30 days is one month later, 31 to 60 days is two months later, and so on.

It leaves out tax, VAT, interest, stock and growth, so it shows the timing gap and nothing else.

Assumptions

Monthly sales
Default: £20,000. The same every month, invoiced from month 1.
Monthly costs
Default: £15,000. The same every month, from month 1.
Days your customers take to pay
Default: 60. Rounded up to whole months, so 60 days means you are paid two months after the sale.
Days you take to pay suppliers
Default: 30. Rounded up to whole months, so 30 days means you pay one month after the cost.
Cash at the start
Default: £10,000. In the bank at the start of month 1, with nothing owed before then.
Time period
Default: 6 months. Each month counts as 30 days.
Payment timing
Default: Whole months. A payment lands the number of days divided by 30, rounded up, months later; 0 days is the same month.
Tax, VAT and interest
Default: None. The explorer leaves out tax, VAT, interest, stock and growth.

Limitations

Illustrative only. Uses no current tax rates or official values, and shows only the timing gap between profit and cash.
